cloze.title: Say it the exam way
cloze.text:
Stellar objects emit radiation over a [[wide range|single value]] of wavelengths. A hotter object has a [[shorter|longer]] peak wavelength. At every wavelength, it emits [[more|less]] energy per unit area per second.

So a red star is [[cooler|hotter]] than a blue star. The cosmic microwave background radiation is evidence for the [[Big Bang|steady state]] theory. So is the dark night sky, known as [[Olbers'|Hubble's]] paradox.

warmup_p2.alt: Hubble's Law states that the universe is expanding. The expanding universe is one piece of evidence that supports the Big Bang theory. (a) State one other piece of evidence that supports the Big Bang theory. 1 mark.

mi.alt: Marking instructions for 2018 Section 2 Question 5(a), 1 mark: cosmic microwave background radiation, or Olbers' paradox, or the abundance of hydrogen and helium in the Universe. Also accepted: the present temperature of the Universe, 2.7 K. Not accepted: the abbreviation CMBR on its own, or further evidence based on redshift alone.

mc.alt: Graphs show radiation per unit surface area R against wavelength for two stars, P and Q. Star Q's curve is higher and peaks at a shorter wavelength. Statements: I Star P is hotter than star Q. II Star P emits more radiation per unit surface area than star Q. III The peak intensity of the radiation from star Q is at a shorter wavelength than that from star P. Which are correct? A I only, B II only, C III only, D I and II only, E II and III only.
fb: Not this one. Star Q's curve is higher and peaks at a shorter wavelength, so Q is the hotter star. I is wrong.
Not this one. Star Q's curve is higher at every wavelength, so Q emits more radiation per unit surface area, not P.
Right. Q's curve peaks further left, at a shorter wavelength. I and II are wrong: Q's curve is higher everywhere, so Q is hotter and emits more.
Not this one. Both I and II are wrong. Q's curve is higher and peaks at a shorter wavelength, so Q is hotter and emits more.
Not this one. III is right, but II is wrong. Q's curve is higher, so Q emits more per unit surface area.

mc.alt: Statements about radiation from stellar objects. I Stellar objects emit radiation over a wide range of frequencies. II The peak wavelength of radiation is longer for hotter objects than for cooler objects. III At all frequencies, hotter objects emit more radiation per unit surface area per unit time than cooler objects. Which are correct? A I only, B III only, C I and II only, D I and III only, E I, II and III.
fb: Not this one. I is correct, but III is correct too: at every frequency, a hotter object emits more.
Not this one. III is correct, but I is too: stellar objects emit over a wide range of frequencies.
Not this one. II is wrong. Hotter objects have a shorter peak wavelength, not a longer one.
Right. I and III are correct. II is wrong: hotter objects have a shorter peak wavelength.
Not this one. II is wrong: hotter objects peak at a shorter wavelength.

mc.alt: A graph shows energy emitted per second per unit area against wavelength for four stars W, X, Y and Z. Star Z's curve is highest with its peak at the shortest wavelength; W's is lowest. Statements: I Star Z is hotter than star W. II The peak frequency of radiation emitted is greatest for star W. III Star Y emits more energy per second per unit area than star X. Which are correct? A I only, B II only, C III only, D I and III only, E I, II and III.
fb: Not this one. I is correct, but III is too: star Y's curve is above star X's, so Y emits more energy per second per unit area.
Not this one. II is wrong. Star W is the coolest. Its peak is at the longest wavelength, so the lowest frequency.
Not this one. III is correct, but I is too: star Z's curve is highest and peaks at the shortest wavelength, so Z is the hottest.
Right. I: Z's curve is highest and peaks at the shortest wavelength, so Z is hotter than W. III: Y's curve is above X's. II is wrong: W is coolest, so its peak frequency is the lowest.
Not this one. II is wrong. Star W is the coolest, so its peak is at the longest wavelength and the lowest frequency.

mc.alt: Cosmic microwave background radiation and Olbers' paradox provide evidence for: A the photoelectric effect, B the Bohr model of the atom, C the theory of special relativity, D the Big Bang theory, E Newton's Law of Universal Gravitation.
fb: Not this one. The photoelectric effect is about light releasing electrons from a metal. These two observations are about the whole Universe.
Not this one. The Bohr model explains line spectra from atoms. These two observations are about how the Universe began.
Not this one. Special relativity is about time dilation and length contraction. These observations are about how the Universe began.

Right. The cosmic microwave background is radiation left over from the hot early Universe. Olbers' paradox, the dark night sky, means the Universe has not been there for ever. Both support the Big Bang.
Not this one. Newton's law is about the gravitational force between masses. These observations are evidence about how the Universe began.

paper2.alt: Stars emit radiation with a range of wavelengths. The peak wavelength depends on the surface temperature of the star. (a) A graph shows energy emitted per second per unit area against wavelength for a star with a surface temperature of 5000 K. A second star has a surface temperature of 6000 K. On the graph, add a line for the second star. 2 marks. (b) A table gives surface temperature T and peak wavelength: 7700 K, 3.76 × 10⁻⁷ m; 8500 K, 3.42 × 10⁻⁷ m; 9600 K, 3.01 × 10⁻⁷ m; 12 000 K, 2.42 × 10⁻⁷ m. Use all the data to show that T = 2.9 × 10⁻³ ÷ peak wavelength. 3 marks.

mi.alt: Marking instructions for 2019 Paper 2 Question 6(a)(b). (a) 2 marks: peak wavelength less (1); the line added is always above the original line (1). (b) 3 marks: T × peak wavelength worked out for all four stars, each about 2.9 × 10⁻³ (2), therefore T × peak wavelength = 2.9 × 10⁻³ (1).

paper2.alt: A student explains the expansion of the Universe using an expanding balloon model. The student draws galaxies on a balloon and then inflates it. Using your knowledge of physics, comment on this model. 3 marks.
paper2.mi_note: The specimen paper's marking for this question is not available. Open-ended questions are all marked on the same scheme: 3 marks for a good understanding, 2 for a reasonable one, 1 for a limited one. Use the marking for 2015 Section 2, Question 5 below.

paper2.alt: A quote from a well-known science fiction writer states: In the beginning there was nothing, which exploded. Using your knowledge of physics, comment on the above statement. 3 marks.

mi.alt: Marking instructions for 2015 Section 2 Question 5, open-ended, 3 marks: 0 marks for no understanding, 1 mark for a limited understanding, 2 marks for a reasonable understanding, 3 marks for a good understanding of the physics involved.
